That power (Śakti) as well, possessing the form of the Kāmakalā and adorned with earrings,
proceeding along the path of Śiva, having pierced through the fourteenth knot;
23a) Having entered, she who possesses a subtle form and essential nature became the supreme guest;
she, moreover, is threefold, manifesting as the creation in the forms of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Having thus reflected, the excellent practitioner shall bring the three worlds under his control. Now, [this is done] by means of the tortoise-mudrā (kūrmamudrā).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: One should join the index finger of the left hand with the little finger of the right,
and likewise the index finger of the right hand with the thumb of the left.
One should extend the right thumb and join the middle and other fingers of the left hand behind the back of the right hand.
Likewise, with the *pitṛtīrtha* of the left hand, we shall place [the water] upon the middle of the nose;
and we shall perform it with the downward-facing palm of the right hand.
One should make the back of the right hand level like the shell of a tortoise;
such a hollow of the palm bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The wise man, having closed both eyes with the heart-mantra,
should remain perfectly steady, keeping the body, head, and neck in a straight line.
One who practices with equanimity like a meditative absorption is a mother; she pervades all evil as a sacrificial fee, and is liberated from the accumulation of faults.
O Mahādeva in the form of Śava, she is seated upon your heart,
surrounded on all four sides by the Śivās with their terrible roars.
And she was seated together with Mahākāla,
intent on amorous pleasure, her eyes serene with bliss, her lotus-like face smiling.
One should always meditate upon Kālikā together with the circle of Yoginīs;
in this way, one should contemplate Kālī, who dwells in the abode of the cremation ground.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the sacrifice. As it is stated in the *Svatantra*:
"One should worship her with mental enjoyments—namely, perfumes, flowers, lamps, and food offerings accompanied by bali—and likewise with mental [offerings]."
Then, indeed, one should perform the mental recitation (jāpya) as well as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth;
having paid homage and made a prayer, this is for the sake of the external sacrifice.

He states the distinction in the *Kālīya*: "By whatever sequence various auspicious substances are used in the Tantra, by that same sequence the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*) is proclaimed for the Bhairavas.
The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*), with all ritual services (*upacāra*), should thus recite the mantra within the mind alone."
One should not display the mudrā there; rather, one should meditate with both hands.
In this case, mounting [the deity] is not desired; worship is performed mentally within the heart.

24a) Regarding "the act of destruction": first, having meditated upon one's own self in the form of *kāmakalā*, and having visualized the *kuṇḍalinī* from the *mūlādhāra* up to the level of *paramaśiva*, one should flood her with the nectar of the moon.
Having taken a flower from a tortoise-shell and led it through the *suṣumṇā*, one who meditates upon the Goddess in the red lotus with eight petals at the heart—
[visualizing her] with a formidable face, terrifying, with disheveled hair, and four arms.
Kālikā, adorned with a divine garland of severed heads, [bestows] the southern [direction].
Her left upper and lower lotus-hands hold a freshly severed head and a sword;
her right lower and upper hands likewise display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons while holding a sickle.
She has the luster of a great cloud, she is dark-complexioned, and likewise she is naked; with a severed head hanging from her neck, it is covered in dripping blood.
Terrifying with a pair of corpses suspended from her ears,
possessing fierce fangs and a gaping mouth, with full and elevated breasts,
wearing a girdle made of a multitude of hands from corpses, and smiling-faced.
Her face is splashed with streams of blood from a pair of severed arms;
she is of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, and dwells in the cremation ground.
Having propitiated Daṃturā with devotion in mind, one should then perform the external worship.
Thus it is said in the Kumārītantra:
"In this manner, one should indeed worship according to the prescribed rite with mental enjoyments, perfumes, flowers, lamps, wine, and offerings."
Then, indeed, one should perform the mental recitation (*jāpya*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) dedicated to Bhairava;
having thus paid homage and offered praise, one should then practice the external yoga.
In the Rudrajāmala.
Now I shall describe the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), which bestows eighteenfold fruits,
by means of which yoginīs are always born as those who do not desire [worldly] names.
One of vast intellect should perform meditation upon the Guru as was done by the ancients;
thereafter, the wise one should perform the ritual bath, whereby Saccidānanda is realized.
One should bathe at the pure holy ford (tīrtha) of Puṣkara, which rests upon the feet [of Viṣṇu];
if a man bathes at any other ford, rebirth exists for him once more.

Having established Kuṇḍalinī at the Mūlādhāra and caused the nectar from the moon on the forehead of Sadāśiva to flow, the flooding of the wheel of the heart (viducakra) means bathing by immersion in that [nectar].
Now follows the mental twilight devotion (mānasandhyā).
In whatever family one is born from the union of Śiva and Śakti,
that [union] is perceived by those established in meditative absorption as the culmination of the Kula-sandhyā.
Thus is the twilight rite (saṃdhyā).
One should offer to one's chosen deity that supreme nectar which is stirred up by the conjunction of the moon, the sun, and the wind,
with that divine nectar.
Thus ends the libation.

The wise one of pure intellect should perform the perfection of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by placing the names of the *liṅgas* upon the support (*ādhāra*), in the heart-lotus, at the root of the throat, and on the forehead; then on the two-petaled, sixteen-spoked, two-leafed, ten-leaved, twelve-fold, and four-fold wheels; then at the end of the *vasu* (the eighth), in the middle of the *bāla* (the first), and together with the *upa* and *paṭa* (the letters *u* and *ṭa*) at the root of the throat; and finally, he should place the vowels, along with *ha* and *kṣa*, in the middle of the staff (*daṇḍa*).
"With the six dhyānas? Thus [are] the internal mātṛkās.
Now follows the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) according to the *Gautamīya*: "Obeisance to the one who is worthy of worship, whose heart is the essence of consciousness;

that [obeisance] is performed with the Heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), preceded by the word 'tat' (That) and followed by the word 'anṛta' (Untruth). [This is done] unto the Supreme Self, whose form is pure consciousness and who is exalted by qualities such as omniscience."
The teachers perform the intake of the sense-objects with the Śiromantra;
it is firm through the heart, the chest, the hips, the left [thigh], and likewise the feet.
The initiation of one's own deity is performed with reverence through the mantra,
by means of the splendor expressed by the mantra within the body that consists of the mantra.
By means of the mantra, this concealment is performed everywhere day by day; it bestows supreme knowledge, which is the nature of pure consciousness, within the Supreme Self.
The splendor consisting of the heart and other centers, which is designated as being right here,
destroys the internal and other forms of the practitioner.
The net of ignorance is said to be the abode of the arrows of Māra;
it is called *saṃvṛti* (conventional reality), which is to be pierced for the sake of protection.
Now, meditation.
One should meditate upon the two lotuses situated within the enclosure of the two powers (śakti) in the Udayākara paddhati,
consisting of the essence of light, through the application of the Kula.
Regarding "the two ornaments": there are two upward-pointing triangular mandalas from the two vessels (*kuṇḍa*).
Then, having filled the body through the contemplation of light, [one contemplates] the state of oneness and the state of equal flavor of Kuṇḍalinī with Śiva and Śivā.
As it has been said:
"The bone situated between two *śṛṅgāṭas* is enclosed by a pair of *śaktis*."
The state of equal flavor (samarasa) is always to be meditated upon; that is the meditation of those yogis who have attained its power.
Thus concludes meditation. Now, the worship.
One should worship with various flowers; at that very moment, one becomes absorbed in That. Also elsewhere:
As it is said in the *Svatantra*:
"One should worship one's own self in the form of the Goddess, the wheel of Śaktis all around, with flowers that are the objects of one's states of being; thus one becomes identical with That."
Also in another tantra:

"The placement [of mantras] (nyāsa) is the realization of identity with that; one should contemplate with the feeling of 'I am He' (so'ham), free from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), passion (rāga), and likewise pride (mada)."
Non-delusion, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-agitation; then the self, the serpent, vitality, and splendor—the wise know these as the ten flowers.
Non-violence is the supreme flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower;
compassion is a flower; patience is a flower; and knowledge is the fifth flower.
Having spoken thus, one should worship oneself as the deity with these supreme flowers,
according to the *Mātṛkā-arṇava*.
The fifty-fold rosary has been described; the thread is of the nature of Śiva, and by means of the knots, the Kuṇḍalinī energy resides at the end of the Kalās within the vital breath.

Now, the fire sacrifice (homa): One should contemplate within the navel the fourfold [selves]—the Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman, and Jñānātman—within a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing a blissful girdle and a semi-circular womb-shaped [altar]. Into the fire kindled by the fuel of the seat, situated in the midst of that, one should offer oblations. This has been stated in the Vaṃhikā and other texts:
In the pit situated at the *mūlādhāra*, blazing with the fire of the deity and joined with merit and demerit, [one should offer] preceded by the root mantra.
The wise one should offer oblations individually, saying "I sacrifice, svāhā!"—
offering as the sacrificial oblation (havis) the ego-sense, malice toward others, backbiting, lust, anger, and so forth.
The *mata* has been declared as the ladle (*śruva*), while the *unmanī* is said to be the sacrificial pit (*gudī*).
Furthermore, other matters should be understood from another tantra; they will become clear in the practical application (*prayoga*).
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice, one becomes directly composed of Brahman;
for such a person, there is neither sin nor merit, and they certainly become liberated while living.

Thus concludes the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): Then, having become a purified *puruṣakalpa* [initiate] through the means of worship, one who has assumed the attire of a woman, marked with vermilion (*sindūra*), adorned with ornaments, and resplendent in dress and the like, with his mouth filled with betel-leaf, should sit upon a lotus posture (*padmāsana*) with a concentrated mind, facing either the east, the north, or the northeast.

"Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh and the left foot beneath the right thigh, by touching both outer sides [of the knees], it is called the lotus posture (padmāsana). Then follows breath control (prāṇāyāma):
having filled the air through the left nostril according to one's capacity, having expelled it through the right, and then again through the right.
Having taken up the wind and gone out through the left nostril, it enters again through the left door sixty-four times;
having drawn in the wind with that seed-syllable *kṛm* and revolved it sixty-four times, one should hold it with that same seed-syllable.
When it has revolved sixteen times, one should accumulate [the merit] in the person.
At the time of *prāṇāyāma*, having meditated upon the seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the form of fire, sun, and moon at the *mūlādhāra*, heart, and *brahmarandhra*,
one should then perform the internal *saṃdhyā* according to the method stated in the previous verse,
ending with the placement of the *saṃsṛkā* and the previously mentioned *karakacchapa* mudrā.
The one to be invoked.
The rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Having visualized [the deity] with the mind as having the previously described form, and having meditated upon her together with her retinue within the lotus of the heart,
one should worship her together with her retinue externally according to the method stated for mental worship, using offerings such as fragrance and so forth.

Having offered the prepared *naivedya* with "Oṃ Namaḥ," at the conclusion of the *naivedya* rite and at the time of one's own meal, one should perform the *anta-vaishvadeva* as follows: [at the *mūlādhāra*].

Having visualized the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front as the form of the Self, the Inner Self, and the Knower of the Self, and having meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī there in the form of the Vedic fire, one should kindle it by fanning with the fuel of good and evil latent impressions (vāsanā).
I offer Dharma into the root [fire], Svāhā! Mūla-mantra: I offer Adharma into the root [fire], Svāhā! Mūla-mantra: I offer "Aham" (the ego) into the root [fire].

Svāhā! Having meditated upon the mind as the *sruva* ladle, well-adorned with flowers, and the mental faculty as the form of the *sruc* vessel, one should recite the mantra according to one's ability—namely: "Untruth, O root! Slander, O root! Desire, O root! Anger and the rest, O root!"—and having offered that recitation to Revatī for the sake of all prosperity, one should perform the ceremonial rinsing (*ācamana*) for the Goddess. [Manasāṃ...]

Having offered a handful of flowers and again meditated upon the *kalā* and *rūpa* according to the teacher’s instruction, having worshipped them through the yoga taught by the teacher, and having remained for a moment in that state of identity with them for the sake of purifying the instruments of action (*karaṇa*), then—
28b) Having raised Kuṇḍalinī according to the method taught by the Guru, having led her to the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta), and having united her with the Supreme Śiva,
one should satisfy the Goddess with the stream of nectar arising therefrom [while displaying] the gestures of the boon (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).

Having displayed the Khaḍga and Muṇḍa mudrās and having prayed for the sake of external worship, one should again become inwardly established in oneself; then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and having meditated upon the self as being cast out by the practice of the weapon-mantra (astramantra), this is the internal sacrifice (antaryāga). As for the manner of displaying the mudrās, it is [described] in the Uttara Tantra.
O Bhairava, the binding with the mudrā should be performed by means of the second Kāmarāja, and the visualization by means of the root mantra.
The abandonment of the mudrā, however, one should effect by means of the *kūrca* seed-syllable;
the *kūrca* seed-syllable is joined with the final vowel [au] preceded and followed by the moon-bindu (*am*).
The *kūrca* seed-syllable is said to be the letter *ha* with the vowel *u* (huṃ).
Having bound the mudrās of the Sugatas with the *kāma* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*) and displayed them with the root-mantra,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the *kūrca* seed-syllable.

29a) Elsewhere it is also stated that there are two kinds [of practice]: the external worship for those who follow the mind and speech, and the internal [worship] for renunciants (nyāsins); for others, it is remembered as being without this [distinction]. Having thus performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), [one performs] the external sacrifice (vahiryāga).

"One should perform [the following]": this is the procedure for the installation of the *argha* vessel. One should place the *kalaśa* to one's left. Having established the support there, one should worship it with: "Obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten digits. Above that, one should worship the digits of fire in a circular form: "Yaṃ, obeisance to Dhūmrārcis" (1); "Raṃ, obeisance to Uṣmā."

Namaḥ || 2 || Jaṃ to Jvalinyai || 3 || Vaṃ to Jvālinyai || 4 || Śaṃ to Visphuliṅginyai || 5 || Ṣaṃ to Suśriyai || 6 || Saṃ to Sarūpāyai || 7 || Haṃ to Kapilāyai || 8 || Laṃ to Havyavahāyai || 9 || Kṣaṃ to Kavyavahāyai || 10 || Having thus worshipped [the fire], one should place upon it a vessel that has not been washed with a string.
Above that, having worshipped with "Obeisance to the solar maṇḍala consisting of twelve digits (kalās)," one should worship the solar digits in a circular form.
29b) Kaṃ Bhaṃ to Napinī (1); Khaṃ Chaṃ to Nāpinaiśāṃyu Dhūmrā (3); Ghaṃ Phaṃ to Marocī (4); Ṅa Naṃ to Jvālinī (5); Vaṃ Dhaṃ to Ruci (6); Chaṃ Daṃ to Supumṛgā (7); Jaṃ...

Having worshipped with *thaṃ* for Bhogadā (8), *saṃ* for Viśvā (9), *jaṃ* for Vodhinī (10), *ṭaṃ* for Dhariṇī (11), and *ṭhaṃ* for Kṣamā (12), and having recited the root Mātṛkā in reverse order while filling the pure surface [of the vessel],
one should worship it with: "Obeisance to the lunar maṇḍala consisting of sixteen kalās."
One should worship the digit of the Moon (somakalā) in a circular form: Aṃ Aṣṭāyai 1; Aṃ Manadayai 2; I Pūryāyai 3; Ī Tuṣṭyayai 4;
Uṃ Puṣpāyai 5; Ū Dhṛtyai 6; Ṛṃ Satvai 7; Ṛṃ Varāśinyai 8; Laṃ Candrikāyai 9; Laṃ Kāyai 10; Eṃ Jyotsnāyai 11; Eṃ Śriyai 12; O Prītyai 13; Auṃ...
Having worshipped with "Aṅgadāyai" (14), "Am Pūrṇāyai" (15), and "Aḥ Pūrṇābhṛtāyai" (16), one should [worship] with the *Ṛk* beginning with "Jātavedase," which is in the *Gāyatrī* meter.

Having consecrated it three times with the root mantra repeated once each, one should visualize a seed-syllable in the form of the Goddess there and worship it with perfume and flowers; this is the procedure for the installation of the pitcher (kalaśa).
Now follows the general offering of water (argha).

Having placed a common copper vessel that has been washed with water and dried, having filled it with the root mantra, having consecrated it eight times with the root mantra, and having worshipped it with scents and flowers using the root mantra, [one offers] water; this is the procedure for the general *argha*.
Now, the procedure for the removal of the special *arghya*: its placement between the *pīḍā* and the *ātman*.
Then the practitioner of mantra should prepare the *argha* offering in a vessel made of conch-shell, copper, or similar material.

Having fashioned there a circle, a triangle, a hexagon, and a square using the *argha* water, he should sprinkle it with water while reciting "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," and worship the center with the root mantra. [Root Mantra]
Having worshipped the triangle with the *Veṇa* mantra, and having worshipped the six syllables in the six corners, one should divide the circle.

Having prepared the fivefold offering with the right-hand ritual sequence: *Oṃ glūṃ, homage to the jewel of the sky; Oṃ ralūṃ, homage to the jewel of heaven; Oṃ aṃstūmatyāralāya, [homage to the jewel]; Oṃ plū, homage to the jewel of the underworld; Oṃ lūṃ, homage to the jewel of the nāgas.* Having thus worshipped, [proceed].

In the square, in the directions starting from the east, having worshipped thus: "Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Kāmarūpa; Oṃ, to the seat of Jālandhara; Oṃ, to the seat of Pūrṇagiri; Oṃ, salutation to the seat of Uḍḍiyāṇa."

There, having placed a tripod washed with the Astra-mantra, one should worship the external maṇḍala endowed with its digits (kalās) upon it as before; then, having placed a copper vessel washed with the Astra-mantra upon that,
and having worshipped the solar maṇḍala and its digits thereon as previously described, [one should recite] the root mantra and the Mātṛkā.

While reciting the *viloma* [inverted] mantra, one should mentally offer nectar (*sudhā*) flowing from the crescent moon between the eyebrows; then, for the purpose of purifying the water with pure water, one should worship within the water with the mantra: *oṃ ṣoḍaśakalātmane somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*.

31a) Above that, having worshipped the sixteen digits (*kalā*) as before, one should offer the *argha* water into the mouth with one's own root mantra— neither with the *pramāṇa-vādina* nor with the *praṇava*. Then, without looking [elsewhere], one should [offer] sandalwood, *japā* flowers, and so forth.

Having placed the eight fragrances [on the vessel], having touched the water consecrated with *acata*, and having empowered it by reciting the root mantra eight times, one should worship the heart, head, crest, armor, and face [of the deity] in the southeast, south, southwest, northwest, and above; then, having worshipped the eyes in the cardinal directions and the weapons in the intermediate directions, one should offer salutation.

Having thus worshipped, covered that water with the *matsya-mudrā*, meditated upon it as the form of the Goddess, recited the mantra seven times over it, protected it with the *astra-mantra*, shielded it with the *kavaca-mantra*, and displayed the *go-mudrā* with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*; then, having performed the *saṃnirodhi-nyāsa* at each junction (*sandhi*) with the seed-syllable *aiṃ*, he displayed the *yoni-mudrā*.

Having contemplated that water as being of the nature of the Goddess, and having reflected upon what is to be done in the interval, one should take up the materials for worship and perform the triple worship of oneself with the root mantra.
Thus is the procedure for the installation regarding the specific purpose. To the north of the *arghya* [vessel],
having drawn four triangular mandalas, upon them are placed the common vessels for the *pādya* and *arghya*.

O Mana, having washed the vessels for the *madhuparka* offering, [place] *dūrvā*, *aviṣṇukrāntā*, and *kaṭu* in the *pādya* vessel; flowers, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and *dūrvā* above the *arghya* vessel;
and in the *ācamana* vessel, the powder of nutmeg (*jātī*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and *kaṅkola*; and in the *madhuparka* vessel—
Having poured in clarified butter, curd, and honey.

There, one should consecrate [the items] with mantras, repeating them once or repeatedly in sequence. Then, on the right side, having arranged a flower-basket, food offerings (naivedya), garments, ornaments, and musical instruments, and having established an oil lamp— if it is a cloudless lamp, it is auspicious— and having set out the vessels for the ritual, one should perform everything according to one's capacity.
And [the vessel] is red; or else, in a single vessel, one should prepare the *argha* and other offerings with *kalāya* beans.

32a) Here, in the absence of substances, one should at this time offer only rice grains according to one's capacity. This is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "In the absence of substances, washed rice grains offered as a gift bring auspiciousness."
Also elsewhere.
"In the absence of substances, one should remember them in the vessels of unhusked rice.
Now follows the yoga of the self.
Then, having filled the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with water, one should worship the deities of the *pīṭha* within one's own body by means of that water in the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*),

in the form of a sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Having worshipped them with scents and flowers, one should visualize the Supreme Deity upon that *pīṭha* and offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the head, heart, navel, feet, and all the limbs.
Having given.

In this regard, the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is as follows: having raised the Kuṇḍalinī from the *mūlādhāra* and caused her to reach the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], one should effect her union there with Śiva; then, having gratified the Goddess with the stream of nectar arising from that union and having visualized the body as consisting of the Goddess, one should perform the external worship, beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with the lamp (*dīpa*).
"No food offering (naivedya) should be given."
32b) Thus it has been said:
One should offer [the worship] even without the offerings of food (naivedya), perfumes (gandha), and other such services.
Thus, all of this—from the vessel of sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī) onwards—should be offered until the heap of flowers; this is the self-worship (ātmapūjā). As it has been said:
"One should collect all of this with water contained in the sprinkling vessel. Thus it is said in the *Vṛhannārāyaṇī-prayogasāra*:
"One who is not Śiva should not practice Śiva; one who is not Śiva should not worship Śiva;
one who is not Śiva should not meditate on Śiva; and one who is not Śiva shall not attain Śiva."
"Having become a god, worship the gods"—so says the Śruti. By this much, one understands the fitness for the qualification of deity-worship.
Now, the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā).
In that regard, one should worship the yantra or the yantra-seat (dhārapīṭha) according to the prescribed method.

Āṃ, to the Ādhāra-śakti; Praṃ, to Prakṛti; above that, Maṃ, to the Maṇipīṭha; in the four directions, to the various hosts of sages (muni-gaṇa), to the various deities (devatā), to the Śavas, to the Śarvas and Muṇḍas, and to the Śivās who delight in many dust and bones.

Having meditated on the lion throne encircled by a jeweled pedestal, [one should worship] in the corners starting from the southeast: "Oṃ Dharmāya Namaḥ," "Oṃ Adharmāya Namaḥ," "Jñāṃ Jñānāya," "Vai Vairāgyāya," and "Aiṃ Aiśvaryāya" in the directions starting from the east.
One should worship Adharma and the others in the four directions: Aṃ to Adharma; Aṃ to Ignorance (Ajñāna); Aṃ to Non-detachment (Avairāgya); Aṃ to Non-perfection (Anaiśvarya);
Aṃ to Ananta; Aṃ to the Lotus (Ambuja); Ā to Bliss (Ānanda); Saṃ to the Pericarp (Karṇikā);
Saṃ to the Universal-Self Lotus (Sarvātmaka-padma); Praṃ to the petals of Primordial Nature (Prakṛti-maya-patra). Viṃ...

Salutation to the filaments consisting of transformations. Paṃ, salutation to the pericarp which is the seed-syllable of the fifty letters. Aṃ, salutation to the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala) whose self consists of twelve digits (kalās). Uṃ, salutation to the lunar disc (somamaṇḍala) whose self consists of sixteen digits. Maṃ, salutation to the fire-disc (vahni-maṇḍala) whose self consists of ten digits. Saṃ, to Sattva. Raṃ, to Rajas. Taṃ...
*Tamase*, *Ām Ātmane*, *Aṃ Antarātmane*, *Paṃ Paramātmane*, *Hrīṃ Jñānātmane*. Then (33b).
There, in the eight principal petals worshipped with milk and filaments, [one proceeds] by way of the center in a clockwise direction.

Having meditated upon the forms resembling fire that is white, black, red, and dark-blue, and those resembling white collyrium, Jayā, and Asanābha-taja, one should worship the Śaktis of the seat—Varā, Abhayā, and Pīṭhaśakti—with the following: *Ī* to Icchā; *Jñā* to Jñānā;

having performed this threefold, he should worship her with red flowers and unguents.

at the end of everything, [one should add] "namah" and the words "I worship Kālī" above the foot.

All of them are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, adorned with garlands, and dancing while holding [the sword] with their left hands; they stand behind Umā.

An ointment, incense, a lamp, and a beverage.

Three times with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains. This has been stated in the Kālītantra:

in that very same place.

The seed-syllables are the initial letters of their names, preceded by *ḍe* and followed by *namaḥ*. In the *Kālikalpa*, having first extracted the word *Śrī*, one should utter the word *pādukā*.
After that, I worship; one should then worship the deities of the limbs.
In the Kumārī-tantra:

Then one should offer incense, lamps,
and food offerings to the Goddess with devotion, especially with fresh flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).
In the independent [tradition].
Then, having again worshipped the Root Goddess with mudrās, libations, and offerings,
and having performed the recitation and bowed down, one should dismiss her into the heart.
In the Kālitantra:

one should repeatedly present the food offering and other gifts to the Goddess according to one's capacity.
In the Kumārī Tantra:

Having meditated upon the Goddess, one should cause Śunaḥśepa to recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
then, one should offer the oblation and the victory of the Goddess into her left hand.
Having recited the mantra, "O you who protect the most secret of secrets," he should then place a flower on his head and prostrate with all eight limbs.
In that interval.
One should gratify the Supreme Deity with musical instruments such as conchs and bells;
one should offer unguents and perform worship with chowries.
One should show a mirror with devotion and offer it again and again;
then one should give betel-leaf together with camphor and other ingredients and sugar.
One should not disparage the circumambulation while reciting the *Karpūra-stuti*;
then, having dismissed [the deity] with supreme devotion by means of the dismissal (*visarjana*) mudrā.
Having brought Kālikā into one's heart, one certainly becomes identical with her;
this has been stated in the Yāmala.
Then all the rites, such as the worship of the *vali* offering, are performed at night;
therein, through the grace of Kālī, the Dakṣa-yajña comes to an end.
Contemplating the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra, the beloved [disciple],
being satisfied and of steady mind, should recite the mantra along with its residual impressions (savāsana).
"Along with the latent impressions (vāsana) in the *Sārtha*; the latent impressions are explained here in the *Uttaratantra*."
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall explain the latent impression (vāsanā) and the determination of reality (tatvanirṇaya):
from the three seed-syllables arises the Śāmbhavī [power], which consists of the energy (kalā) of the letter 'va' along with the vowel 'i'.
By means of just two lines of the heart [mantra], she brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
by means of the two seed-syllables of sound, she awakens the mass of sounds.
This Great Vidyā, whose nature is eternal consciousness, remains ever awake even when there are no words of address; she shines forth as pure, absolute Consciousness alone.
Arising from the two seeds as both meaning and sound, yet devoid of objective existence—
reciting the mantra with a serene mind while remembering its meaning within a pure heart, one should practice it according to the revelation of Mantra and Tantra.
Thus it has been said:
One should recite the mantra attentively, neither too fast nor too slow.

This has been stated in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:

then, having offered a prostration, one should extract the seed-syllable of Hṛllekhā Kaulinī.

"Or whatever else has been told by me, O Lord— tell me, what is its nature? The Lord said:
O Goddess, Maheshani, out of affection for you, this most secret of secrets is told; without which, indeed, there is no victory and so forth, even if one is free from parts.
The *kullūrka* of Tārā is the goddess Mahānīla Sarasvatī;

O Supreme Goddess, the mantra of Kālī beginning with *kūrca* (huṃ) and ending with *vadhūḥ* (strīṃ) and *phaṭ* is the eight-syllabled *kullukā* of Chinnamastā, O Great Sovereign.
One should proclaim the hide at the end of the *vajra* and the *vairocanīya*.
First is the Kullukā-mantra of Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity;
then the twelve-syllable Kullukā of the illustrious Tripurasundarī.
First is the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, immediately after that the Kāmarāja,
then the Lajjā seed-syllable, and after that Tripureśī.
After the word "Bhagavati," one should extract the syllable "dvam" at the end;
thus has the Goddess been described by me in brief.
41a) Having understood this, if a foolish warrior exerts himself in vain within the realm of desire, he quickly meets his death and the loss of accomplishment (siddhi) occurs.
The mantras become averse and the loss of accomplishments occurs;
therefore, all recitations and other rites will be flawless—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should diligently apply the *kullukā* upon the head.
Now, I shall explain that further; listen, O Priyaṃvadā.
Through knowledge of which recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites do not become fruitless;
it is the bridge for Brahmins by means of the *praṇava*, and likewise for Kṣatriyas as well.
O Goddess of the gods, it is said that for Vaiśyas the mantra consists of the syllable *phaṭ*, while for a Śūdra it is *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*).
O Mistress of the gods, he who recites this mantra with the *aja* (the syllable *oṃ*) in his heart [attains success].
Indeed, he has no authority over any mantras whatsoever, O Goddess;
for she is Mahālakṣmī, the beautiful mistress of the world.
The seed-syllable of Kālikā is the one ending in *surānta* (the letter *r*), while that of Tārā is the one ending in *vaktra* (the letter *v*).
For the others, however, O fair-faced one, the seed-syllable is *vadhu* (the letter *dh*) and the Great Bridge (*mahāsetu*).
Having first recited the Mahāsetu, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
[thereby] one becomes a lord of wealth, a lord of movement, a lord of speech, and a master of eloquence.
O Kṛtānta-like one, for women who are like the goddess Umā, and for those resembling Madana, this shall be the time for recitation;
there is no doubt that it is the time for recitation.
Now I shall explain Nirvāṇa; listen attentively, O sinless one!
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then recite the Mātṛkā-gha.
Then, O Great Goddess, one should utter the root mantra, followed by the Vībhava;
then the entire Kāmātṛkā, and again one should utter the Praṇava.
Thus, one should recite the mantra with the root syllable encapsulated during the practice of *pūraka*;
such is the power of this [mantra], which even Yama does not know.
For even with a hundred [repetitions], success does not arise for one who is distracted;
therefore, O Maheśvarī, one should practice with every effort that which has been taught.
Then, according to the rules of practice, one should mutter the unsurpassed mantra;
[one should know] the seer, the meter, the deity, the seed-syllable, the power, and the Kālīka.
O Goddess, one should meditate with diligence and then recite the mantra beginning with *tatsat*;
if one thus recites this unsurpassed king of mantras.
42a) One obtains a celestial mansion [lasting] for a hundred years; there is no need for further deliberation regarding this act of policy.
He himself is directly the sovereign of the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
He alone is the refuge, the knower of all sciences, and the one who understands the reality of mantras;

By the mere sight of him, enemies flee;

having performed it thus, one should first join the King of Mantras folded together. Having reached the end of the *kullukā* in that state of Nirvāṇa, which is honored by the world, the entire world becomes like that for them.

Then, having drawn circular mandalas within the triangles in the east, south, west, and north of the wheel;

[one should contemplate: whether they are above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) or in the expanse of the sky and heavens, on the surface of the earth, in the Kinkama cave, or in the netherworld (pātāla), or wherever they may reside— whether in a field (kṣetra), a seat (pīṭha), or a secondary seat (upapīṭha)— they have set foot there.
O Lord of Heroes, may the goddesses, always honored by us with incense, lamps, and other offerings according to the rite of the auspicious bali, protect us;
[to] the Yoginīs in the Vīrendra-bandha, svāhā! To all the Yoginīs, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! This bali is for the Yoginīs; obeisance!

having meditated upon the Goddess together with her attendants within the heap of flowers— she who is easily accessible through devotion— one should [proceed].

O Supreme Goddess, whose nature is consciousness, O Beloved of the nectar of the supreme state,

Outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) along with their respective weapons.
53a) Oṃ laṃ iṃ ī śrīpādukāṃ; oṃ raṃ agni śrīpādukāṃ; oṃ saṃ yama śrīpādukāṃ;
oṃ kṣaṃ nir-ṛti śrīpādukāṃ; oṃ vaṃ varuṇa śrīpādukāṃ; oṃ yaṃ vāyu.

The *śrīpādukā* of Oṃ Śaṃ So; the *śrīpādukā* of Ahaṃ Īśāna; the *śrīpādukā* of Nirṛti and Varuṇa in the middle; the *śrīpādukā* of Oṃ Hrīṃ Aṃ Naṃ Taṃ in the middle of Ī and Īśāna; and the *śrīpādukā* of Āṃ Brahmā. This has been stated in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā.
Then, having fully worshipped the eight [deities], one should worship Viṣṇu in the southwest, Brahmā in the northeast,
and others elsewhere as well.
It is considered [to be established] by the five, beginning with Indra, who are led by the infinite Brahman.
Having worshipped with the sixty [deities] beginning with Balā and others situated near the wheels and lotuses,

one should take a handful of flowers with the root mantra and offer it while reciting "abhīṣṭasiddhi... Having thus offered the flower-oblation for the worship of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇārcana) and presented the previous worship, one should meditate upon the vajra and other [emblems] within the square mandala and worship as follows:
The Vidyuts are proclaimed to be yellow, pearl-white, black, red, white, and black; they have the luster of a cluster of Kuravinda flowers and are swift-moving.

The sky is blue-colored; *nīlapuṣpāntasīprāya* means a tree with blue flowers, namely the *kuraviṃda*; [the deity] has the color of that flower. *Oṃ vaṃ*, the venerable sandals of the Vajra; *oṃ śaṃ*, the venerable sandals of the Śakti; *oṃ daṃ*, the venerable sandals of the Daṇḍa;
*oṃ khaṃ*, the venerable sandals of the Khaḍga; *oṃ paṃ*, the venerable sandals of the Paśu.
Oṃ, to the goad, the venerable sandal; Oṃ, to the mace, the venerable sandal; Oṃ, to the trident, the venerable sandal.

Oṃ caṃ, the discus, the venerable sandals. Oṃ paṃ, the lotus, the venerable sandals. Having worshipped thus, and having taken a handful of flowers with the root mantra, [one says]: "O Ṣaṣṭhī, may my desired success be granted; this is the worship of the enclosure. Having offered the handful of flowers and presented the previously mentioned [offerings], one should then worship the weapons of the Goddess as follows: Oṃ Śrī Kaṃ above the left.
[The left] upper [hand] is the sword, the *śrīpādukā*. Below that is *oṃ* muṇḍa *śrīpādukā*. The left lower [hand] is the *abhaya* [mudrā], the *śrīpādukā*;

the right upper [hand] is *oṃ* vara *śrīpādukā*. Here, in this [form], the right lower [hand] is the *vara* [mudrā], and the right upper [hand] is the *abhaya* [mudrā]. This is according to the various divisions of the tantras and the various differences in visualization (*dhyāna*). As follows:
And the determination of the Guru’s instruction is stated in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
With her lotus-like hands raised toward her head, she was suddenly blinded by the dazzling brilliance.
The right hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, one below and one above.
In the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*, in the *Kālī Tantra*, and also in the *Mahālakṣmī-stava*.
In her upper left hand she holds a sword at the level of her lotus-palm, and likewise a severed head in the lower [left hand].
In the right [hands] are the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting; O Hara, today [I meditate on] Kālikā in the right [hand]. [This concludes the meditation on the hands.]
In the Bhairavī Tantra, however, it is indeed otherwise.
With her two upper lotus-hands she holds a sword and a freshly severed head;
her two lower lotus-hands likewise display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala:
Then, having worshipped the goddess, one should subsequently worship the weapons in their proper order.
In her left hands she holds a sword and a severed head, and in her right hands she displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, according to the secret [tradition].
54a) She holds a sword and a severed head in her left [hand], and according to the statement, she bestows fear in her right [hand].
Then, [visualize] the sword and skull held above and below, and the hands granting the gestures of fearlessness and boons; having worshipped again with the root mantra.

Having displayed the mudrās of the sword and so forth with the root mantra, and having recited the aforementioned Mahākāla mantra, [worship] "Mahākāla Śrīpādukā. Thus, having worshipped Mahākāla three times to the right of the Goddess.

Having recited the root mantra, one should worship with the words: "Obeisance to Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with her limbs (sāṅgā), together with her retinue (saparivārā), and accompanied by Mahākāla. Having thus worshipped, one should worship again with perfumes and other offerings as follows, at the end of the root mantra:
O Supreme Goddess, out of your grace, accept this supreme fragrance, which fills the quarters of space with the sweet scent of supreme bliss.

Having offered perfume with the words, "Obeisance to Dakṣiṇakālikā together with Śrī Mahākāla," and having presented the perfume-gesture (gandhamudrā) by joining the little finger and the thumb, [recite] the root mantra at the end.
Accept this supreme flower, born from the fourth caste, enchanting with its various qualities and possessing intense fragrance.

"Śrī Mahākāla-sahitāyai Dakṣiṇakālikāyai puṣpāṇi vaiṣaṭ. Having thus offered flowers three times with the index finger and thumb, one should display the flower-mudrā (puṣpa-mudrā) by turning the index finger and thumb downward during the sacrifice. Regarding that, the prohibited [flowers] have been stated as follows:
In the Nīlatantra:
"With various offerings and oblations, with various delightful flowers,
with leaves of Apāmārga and Bhṛṅga— excluding Tulasī leaves."
54b) Devotion is always to be honored, for it surely brings swift results;
the worship of the Goddess is always [effective], even with water, lotuses, or leaves.
"With a mind free from devotion, whether by means of [actions] prescribed or prohibited," according to the *Phetkārī-tantra*.
Whether it be a flower, a leaf, or a fruit, one should never offer it with its face turned downward; such an offering is declared to cause suffering, for as the mantra is, so is the presentation.
Offering flowers face-down is not desired in the rite of the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*);
however, in all *lakṣa-pūjās*, one should offer each flower individually.
If the worship is performed as a collective offering, that is not the case for the presentation of one hundred thousand flowers.

Therefore, having sprinkled the incense vessel with "phaṭ" and offered a flower with "namaḥ," while touching it with the left index finger and reciting the root mantra: "The essence of the forest tree, delightful and bestowing union, may it grant success."
"O you who drink the fragrance, accept this incense which always brings splendor.

I offer this incense to Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with her limbs, her retinue, and Mahākāla; obeisance. Having thus sprinkled the water from the conch, one should perform the *abhyukṣaṇa* (sprinkling) using the thumb and ring finger joined together.
Having displayed the incense mudrā, [one should say]: "Oṃ jayadhvani mantramānaḥ svāhā.

Then, while ringing with the left hand the bell that has been worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, and while praising and proclaiming the fame of the qualities of the deity, one should offer incense to the Goddess. As it is said:
Then, having uttered "O Mother,
recite the mantra," and having worshipped while ringing the bell, one should then fumigate with excellent incense.
55a) Then, having sprinkled the lamp-vessel with "praḍit," and having offered a flower with "namaḥ," one should touch it with the middle finger while reciting the root mantra.
This great lamp, brilliantly radiant, the omniscient one who removes all fear—
may this lamp, which is light both external and internal, be accepted.
Thus, having offered the water from the conch with the words: "Salutation, I offer this lamp to the venerable Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā together with her limbs (retinue)," one should pour it out.
Having displayed the lamp-mudrā by joining the middle finger with the thumb,
and sounding the bell as before, one should display [the gestures] from the eyes down to the feet.
Then, having drawn a triangular maṇḍala in front, [one should offer] "Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the maṇḍala of the sacrificial offering for Dakṣiṇakālī."

Having thus worshipped the maṇḍala, one should place there a vessel provided with a base, containing *māyā*, joined [with other substances], and filled with flowers; then, having displayed the *tatvamudrā* over it, [one recites] at the end of the root mantra:

"Oṃ krīṃ, svāhā to the glorious Dakṣiṇā Kālikā; this is the offering (bali), obeisance. Having thus offered [the water] for sprinkling, O Maheśvarī, one should offer a tula (tobacco leaf) at the beginning of worship, eating, and so forth. Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should prepare a triangular mandala divided into four parts before the food offering (naivedya).
Having honored [it] with "Namaḥ," one should sprinkle [it] there with water from the *dhāraṇī* (55b),
display the *vakramudrā*, and meditating on the wind-seed syllable (*vāyubīja*) "Yam" on the left palm, recite it seven times.
Having dried up the defect of the net of wind arising from that [breath], having selected the seed-syllable (*vīja*) on the right palm,
and having placed the left palm upon my back and forehead, one should display the food offering (*naivedya*). Then,
having selected the seed-syllable "yam" on the left palm as the path for drying up the defects arising from that [offering], it becomes fixed at the point of emanation (*sṛṣṭalagna*).
Having placed the palm of the right hand over the food offering (naivedya) and visualized it as being flooded by a rising stream of nectar,

one should sprinkle the water with the root mantra. Having meditated upon it as being of the nature of nectar and touched it, one should recite the root mantra eight times and display the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings before the deity and offered a handful of flowers, one should meditate that light has issued forth from its mouth;
then, touching the vessel of the food offering (naivedya) with the thumb and ring finger, and taking water with the *kṣa* syllable:
"O Lord of Discernment, I offer this well-prepared *suharvī* (a type of grain) of various and manifold kinds at the end of the root mantra;
please accept it along with your followers. Thus ends the verse (56a).

Having recited [the mantra], one should offer the food oblation (naivedya) with the words: "I offer this food oblation to the auspicious Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with the Mahākāla, along with her limbs (sāṅgāyai), her retinue (saparivārāyai), and salutations (namaḥ). Having thus offered water, one should display the food-oblation mudrā (naivedya-mudrā).
Saying "Oṃ, you are the spreading of nectar, svāhā," he should give water into the hand of the Goddess.

Then, having displayed the *grāsamudrā* resembling a full-blown utpala lotus with the left hand, one should display the *prāṇa* and other mudrās along with the *samatra* with the right hand, as follows:
Oṃ prāṇāya svāhā—with the thumb, little finger, and ring finger.
Oṃ apānāya svāhā—thus [one offers] with the thumb, index finger, and middle finger.
Oṃ vyānāya svāhā—thus [he offers] with the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger.
Oṃ udānāya svāhā—[this is for] the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and navel.
*Oṃ samānāya svāhā*—with this [mantra], using all the fingers beginning with the thumb. Then, at the end of the root mantra:
"I offer water to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with her limbs, her retinue, and accompanied by Mahākāla;
obeisance. At the end of the root mantra...
Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods, the supreme bestower of all satisfaction.
O Amṛtānanda, accept this excellent water in its entirety.
56b) Having thus offered water and perceived the area containing the curtain, the vessels, and the ground,
[he beholds] the Lord being surrounded on all sides by Brahmā, Īśa, and others, and being honored with showers of nectar by the divine maidens.

At that time, having meditated upon the Great Goddess— who delights in jesting and play, who restrains the assembly of those eating in rows, and who enjoys [the offerings]— one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) as an ancillary part of the worship. Therein, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit by the span of one's own right hand,
square, four finger-breadths in height, possessing the prescribed characteristics, and triangular.

Having formed a triangular enclosure with the *kuḍa* [mudrā], one should gaze at it with the *mūla-mantra*. Sprinkling it with water while pronouncing "kaḍi," one should strike it with darbha grass while saying "huṃ. Then, sprinkling with the fist while reciting the *mūla-mantra*, one should establish the fire there, meditate upon the Goddess, and worship her with perfumes and other offerings. [Then offer] with clarified butter: *oṃ mūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ*.

Having offered four oblations with "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā," having offered twenty-five oblations with the root mantra (mūla), and having again offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis, one should worship the deity with perfumes and other offerings.
Having joined [the fire] upon the pedestal, one should dismiss the fire.
O Agni, O you of great power, who accomplishes all tasks!
"Even when another task has arrived, grant your presence with respect."

Then, having drawn a square and triangular maṇḍala on the southern side, one should invoke the Goddess there with the root mantra and worship her with flowers and consecrated rice. "Ehyehi, O Mother of the worlds! Protect the people of the world; accept, accept this offering of meat-rice (sāmiṣānna). Grant success, cause the destruction of enemies, kuru kuru! Hraṃ hraṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ!"
Svāhā! This is the offering for Dakṣiṇakalikā; homage, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ hraṃ!
O Mahākāla, lord of the cemetery, accept this offering of meat and food, accept it twice!
Grant me protection from obstacles and bestow upon me spiritual accomplishment, svāhā!

"This is the bali offering for Mahākāla; homage! Having thus presented the bali to Mahākāla, and then perceiving that the Goddess is satisfied, one should consecrate the water with the *dhenumudrā* and offer water into the hand of the Goddess with the mantra: "Thou art the covering of nectar, svāhā."
Then,
having established the radiant, knowable [deity] of the Nairṛtya direction with the syllable *hraṃ*,
and having caused [the practitioner] to perform the washing of hands and other preliminary rites, [one should offer] to the Southern Kalikā together with Śrī Mahākāla at the root mantra.
I offer betel-leaf; obeisance! [Obeisance to her] who is shimmering with the fragrance of tamāla leaves, camphor, and pūga-nuts.

Having offered the statement, "Please accept this dried and fragrant betel leaf," with the *tatva-mudrā*, one should then display the *cakramudrā* over the eight-petaled lotus made from wheat flour and other materials, which is well-prepared and adorned with gold. Having rendered it nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should worship it with the root mantra: *Oṃ*.
Furthermore, the head is at the root of this [finger].
O you who are accompanied by the assembly of the circle of the Yoginīs of the head, grant the three subtle atoms [of the breath] along with the water of the house for the sake of mental perfection.

With this mantra, preceded by the sounding of the bell and other instruments, one should loudly recite the hymn of praise to the Goddess. Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root seed-syllable and having executed the previously mentioned ṛṣi-nyāsa, chandas-nyāsa, and the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) nyāsa;
58a) Having brought the rosary, one should place it either on a cloth or in the left hand; then, having consecrated it with water from the root-mantra, one should sprinkle it up to the navel.
O Māle, O Māle, O Mahāmāyā, you whose essential nature is all-powerful!
Since you are established as the four castes, therefore, grant me success.

Having worshipped with this mantra using both fragrance and flowers, one should take [the garland] with the right hand while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ Gaṃ, perform the removal of obstacles, O garland! Then, meditating on the Guru at the head, the mantra as being yellow in color at the throat, and the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) at the heart, one should place it upon the heart.

Taking the rosary near the heart and placing it upon the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand, one should recite the Mahākāla mantra— *oṃ hrīṃ smīṃ hraṃ mahākālāya hauṃ mahādevāya krāṃ kālikāyai hau*—
one hundred and eight times, and [dedicate] the fruit of that recitation.

[Offer] the food offering (naivedya) in the hand of Mahākāla. Therein, first, one should place the *kullukā* on the head; having meditated upon the *mahāsetu* in the heart, and having meditated upon *nirvāṇa* in the *viśuddhi* at the *sahasrāra*, one should place it in the *maṇipūra*.
58b) At the Kullukā-bridge, one should construct a great bridge and recite the mantras ten times each. Those mantras are as follows:

*Krīṃ hraṃ strīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ* is the *kullukā*. *Oṃ* is the bridge (*setu*). *Krīṃ* is the great bridge (*mahāsetu*). *Oṃ aṃ krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hraṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ dakṣiṇe kālike krāṃ krāṃ krāṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā aiṃ aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ*.

Having recited "Oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ āṃ" for the sake of Nirvāṇa, one should then [perform] the previously mentioned meditation on the meaning of the mantra, preceded by the assumption of the seat.

"Intent on divine contemplation, one should recite the knowledge preceded by the *praṇava*. Then, having uttered the *praṇava* again and completed the recitation: "O Rosary (*mālā*), you who grant pleasure and auspiciousness to all the gods, be so;
O auspicious one, always bring me good fortune and ward off obstacles for the animal [sacrifice]. *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to success (*siddhi*). Thus [he should say].

Having placed the rosary on one's head with the mantra, and having again performed three rounds of *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform the assignment of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, as well as the six-limbed assignment (*kara-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), [placing it] in the left hand of the Goddess.

"Today, with water, accept this recitation (*japa*), O Goddess, the most secret of secrets; may the *siddhi* of the recitation performed by me be attained through your grace, O Great Sovereign (*Maheśvarī*). Having thus offered [the rosary] to the Goddess and presented a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should then worship the rosary in a secluded place with the five-syllable mantra: *hrīṃ siddhyai namaḥ*.
"One should establish."
Then, having praised him with the Karpūra-stava, one should offer as an oblation (naivedya) jackfruit, coconuts, mangoes, and other fruits according to their availability.

Having bowed down and offered the services with the root mantra, it is said: "One should perform circumambulations while reciting the Karpūra-stuti and the Yāmala. Then, having recited the hymns, the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), the thousand names (*sahasranāma*), and so forth, and having performed circumambulations and prostrations, one should [offer] with water from the *culaka* vessel as follows: *itaḥ pūrvam...* (from this point on).

By virtue of the authority over the vital breath, the intellect, the body, and the qualities, [one acts] through mind, speech, and action— with the two hands, the feet, the anus, and the genitals— during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
May all that has been heard, that has been remembered, that has been spoken, and whatever else there is—all that be offered to Brahman; svāhā!

"May this [offering], along with myself and everything belonging to me, be pleasing to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā. Om tat sat—thus, with the mantra of offering to Brahman, one should dedicate oneself. Then, having accepted the grace bestowed by the Goddess and meditated upon her as the form of light, one should [dissolve] the hosts of the retinue, including the deities of the door and others, into the body of the Goddess.
Having visualized them as dissolved.
O Supreme Goddess, go, go from the root to the supreme abode, to your own station!
Wherein the gods, beginning with Brahmā, know [it] as the supreme state.
Having extracted the *tejasa* (vital energy) from the *nirmālya* flower with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, having smelled it and brought it to the heart through the practice of *pūraka* (inhalation),

one should worship it mentally, contemplate its identity with oneself for a moment, and then establish that energy— transformed into the form of *kuṇḍalinī*— in the *mūlādhāra*. As it is said in the *Svacchanda Tantra*:
Then, one should remember that the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) for the goddess, having dissolved through the differentiation of the functions within the bodies,
become absorbed by means of the root mantra and are placed within the limbs of the goddess.

60a) Then, having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) beginning with the *ṛṣi*, one should fashion a triangular and quadrangular mandala with water in the northeast; having worshipped it with the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*), one should there [recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvarī. Thus.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should set aside a portion for the *naivedya*—specifically a thousandth part—and offer that *naivedya* and so forth into that water with the appropriate mantra. Then, having dismissed the deities residing in the vessel of the *bali* offering with the *narāca-mudrā*, one should perform the dispersal of the *bali*. As follows:

Having placed the mantra of the previously established *vali* vessel into a single bowl, and having first uttered the mantra *Laṃ* outside the worship hall, one should cast that food there while reciting: *ucchiṣṭabhairava ehyehi valiṃ gṛhṇa 2 huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should pray: "Whatever flaw in the sacrifice, whatever flaw in the austerity, whatever flaw..."
O Lord, by Your grace, may all that pertains to my mind in this worship be free from defect.
60b) Having thus ascertained that there is no flaw and having offered the special *argha* water, one should place a flower upon it; then,
on smooth ground, one should draw the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīḥ*) with the little finger of the hand, [and recite] the root-mantra *yaṃ*.
I touch this path with my feet as I behold it with my eyes.
May he protect those who are devoted to him, even if they were equal to Śakra himself.

Having applied the *tilaka* with this mantra, and having placed the unguent and the *nirmālya* (flower offering) upon one's head—after discarding the ordinary *nirmālya* in a clean place—one should meditate upon oneself as the Goddess. This is the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
Now, if one is unable to perform it in such detail, O Śakra, one should rise early in the morning, perform the purification rites (*śaucādi*), and so forth.
Having remembered and bowed to the Guru-devī, and having bathed according to the prescribed method, one who is capable of crossing over [saṃsāra] should,
after the bath for removing impurities, sprinkle water three times on one's own head with the root mantra using the *kumbha-mudrā*.
Having performed the twilight libations (*saṃdhyā-tarpaṇa*) according to the prescribed rule, one who is unable to do so at that time should recite the root mantra nine times in the morning,

thirty-six times at midday, and eighteen times in the evening; then, having offered libations to the Goddess twenty-eight times with the root mantra and having made the *sūryārghya* offering with the root mantra—
Having gone home, one should perform the worship of the maṇḍala according to the previously described method; or, if that is not possible, one should sprinkle the pavilion with the root mantra.

61a) Having prepared a seat there, one should worship the seat with the mantra: *hrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye kamalāsanāya namaḥ*. Then, having purified the disciple’s vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the ritual substances, and having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), [one proceeds].

Even in the *bhūtaśuddhi* (purification of the elements), if one is unable to perform it in detail, one should meditate on the Puruṣa according to the previously mentioned method; then, having dried that body with the seed-syllable *yam* through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), burned it with the seed-syllable *ram*, and dissolved it with the seed-syllable *vam*, one should contemplate the arising of a body in the form of the Goddess, complete with all its limbs, by means of the mantra *īm*.

Having performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) by reciting the mantra twelve times, and having performed the *saṃvinyāsa*; or, if that is impossible, having performed the *ṛṣyādinyāsa*, the *khaḍganyāsa*, and the *mantrākṣaranyāsa*; and having performed the previously mentioned *yogapīṭhanyāsa*;
or, if that is impossible, having installed the nine seats (*navapīṭha*) and the *śakti*, and having meditated according to the previously mentioned [description].

Having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) according to the previously stated method, or— if that is impossible— having meditated upon it and worshipped with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using the root mantra; having contemplated identity with that for a moment and displayed the mudrās,
one should cover the previously mentioned vessels and the water-pot (kalaśa).

61b) Having placed a water vessel on one's own left with the *mūla-mantra* and having worshipped it with the *mūla-mantra*, one should arrange the previously mentioned two types of *argha*— the general and the specific— and perform the services such as the foot-washing (*pādya*) using the general *argha*.

One should prepare [the offerings]. In the event of inability to do so, having placed the vessel for the *arghya* or the vessel for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇī*), one should prepare the water for the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, and other items using the water from the sprinkling vessel itself. Then, having performed the preliminary worship of the attendants (*upamātṛkā-pūjā*), in the event of inability to do so, one should sprinkle one's own body with the root mantra; this is suitable for the worship of the Goddess, as one has become the form of the Goddess.

Having meditated as before and performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*), or in its absence, having worshipped the nine powers of the pedestal (*navapīṭhaśakti*)— eight in the eight directions and one in the center— and having worshipped the corpse-seat (*pretāsana*) in the center with the mantra, one should, upon it,

perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and everything up to the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) according to the previously stated method, preceded by the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
Having performed what was prescribed and established [the deity] with the root mantra,

one should worship the Goddess joined with Mahākāla with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra). At the conclusion of that, having offered three oblations (vali) to all beings, primarily to Mahākāla, [one should perform] the Kullukā-setu.
Having established the Mahāsetu and Nirvāṇa as before,

one should recite the Mahākāla mantra ten times and then recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times. If one lacks the capacity for that, having recited the Mahākāla mantra twenty-seven times along with the root mantra, one should [perform the rite] according to the previously mentioned method using the *saṃhāramudrā*.
Having dismissed the form of the Goddess from oneself, one should meditate upon the Self [as the Goddess]. If one is unable to perform this, then at the time of the *mātṛkā* [mantra],
having meditated on the Guru and having meditated on the Goddess, becoming absorbed in Her for that moment, one should bathe according to the rules of one's own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*),
sprinkle oneself three times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), perform the Vedic *saṃdhyā* ritual, and recite the root mantra nine times.
Having recited the mantra for the four [deities] beginning with the Guru, and having offered libations with the root mantra,
one should meditate upon the Goddess within the solar orb, offer the *argha* water, and having returned home, sprinkle the seat with the root mantra.
Having sat there, performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, visualized the form of the Goddess within one's own body,

performed the *ṛṣi*-vidyā and the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) on the hands, meditated as previously described, and worshipped mentally, one should offer a single *arghya* vessel while reciting: "Obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of the ten digits of the moon."

Having worshipped with "O Support," and having placed the vessel upon it after it has been washed over with the Astra-mantra; having worshipped with "Haṃ, obeisance to the solar orb consisting of twelve kalās," and having filled it with water while reciting the root mantra in reverse order— or while uttering the Vajra-mantra— having taken a little of that water into another vessel...

Having sprinkled the ritual implements and oneself with water, and having worshipped the powers of the seat (*pīṭha-śakti*) and the corpse-seat (*pretāsana*) as before, one should invoke [the deity] with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and arrange the offerings. Having worshipped as before, and having offered the three circumambulations at the conclusion of the food offering (*naivedya*) as before, one should perform the dismissal (*udvāsana*) as previously described; this is the third ritual procedure.
Thus ends the second flower in the *Kālikalpalatā*, composed by the venerable Vimarśānandanātha.
It is finished. May there be auspiciousness.
In the year 1754, on the second day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, it was written at the auspicious site of Lalita in the midst of Nepal.
